sections.heading: Undergraduate Excellence in Research Program
sections.text: The Excellence in Research Program at UC Irvine offers undergraduate students a transformative opportunity to apply classroom knowledge to real-world challenges. Working with top-tier scientists and state-of-the-art facilities, students contribute to cutting-edge research and can present their findings at the Undergraduate Research Symposium. Successful participants receive the prestigious “Excellence in Research” designation and have their work published in the Journal of Undergraduate Research in the Biological Sciences, setting the stage for their future careers.

sections.heading: Biography
sections.text: At UCLA, he co-founded the Burroughs Wellcome Fund Inter-School Program in Metabolic Disease, then one of the few cross-disciplinary doctoral programs in the U.S. aimed at educating scientists capable of integrating population-based quantitative disciplines with laboratory-based sciences. He has mentored and supervised >100 undergraduate, graduate, and post-doctoral fellows. Dr. Liu is an elected fellow/member of several medical societies including the AHA, ASCI, and the American Epidemiological Society (AES). He has also served as a consultant for several national and international authorities addressing medicine, nutrition, and public health issues.

sections.heading: Current Projects/Studies
sections.text: Outside of his role at UC Irvine, Roby co-founded and continues to conduct research at the UC Berkeley/UCLA California Simulation of Insurance Markets (CalSIM) , an initiative dedicated to helping health policy stakeholders and Covered California understand how policy changes may affect different populations through modeling. Recently and most notably, his work at CalSim has been used to estimate the impact of state-based reforms to expand subsidies, reinstate the “individual mandate,” and expand eligibility for Medi-Cal coverage for undocumented young adults.

sections.heading: Biography
sections.text: Dr. Sean Arayasirikul (they/them) is a Medical Sociologist and an Associate Professor In-Residence in the Department of Health, Society, and Behavior (DHSB) at UCI’s Program in Public Health (PPH). Dr. Arayasirikul was a National Institute for Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) T32 Pre-Doctoral Fellow at the Alcohol Research Group, UC Berkeley, an American Sociological Association Minority Fellow (Cohort 38), a Diversity Scholar of the Adolescent Medicine Trials Network for HIV/AIDS Interventions, and an Inter-CFAR Implementation Science Fellow at Johns Hopkins University. Currently, Dr. Arayasirikul is an Associate Director of the University of California Global Health Initiative (UCGHI) Center for Gender and Health Justice (CGHJ), a Board Member of the Society for Implementation Research Collaboration (SIRC), and a Robert Wood Johnson Foundation Interdisciplinary Research Leaders Fellow.

sections.heading: Research and Scholarship Interests
sections.text: Dr. Arayasirikul’s research interrogates the social etiology and root causes of health among sexual and gender minoritized communities. They believe in the transformative power of community-engaged research, digital technologies, and homegrown interventions. They are focused on the following lines of inquiry: 1)	the examination of health disparities and inequity among sexual and gender minoritized (SGM) communities, particularly trans women, BIPOC communities, and those with intersectional identities; 2)	the development and implementation science of systems-level, digital health interventions; and 3)	liberatory applications of participatory approaches to surveillance, data democratization, and health justice. For a list of published work on PubMed: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/myncbi/1xM98YsP9VoAb/bibliography/public/. UCI students interested in getting involved in this work are encouraged to complete an interest form: https://forms.gle/GF5WhUhJcpLaYJm17.

sections.heading: Biography
sections.text: Brandy Lipton, PhD is an applied microeconomist specializing in health economics with additional interests in labor and public economics . Her research uses quasi-experimental methods to examine how health care policies shape health and economic outcomes, with a particular focus on state-level Medicaid programs. Major themes running through her work include (1) Medicaid program design including eligibility policies, optional benefits, and payment structures, ( 2 ) access to preventive health services including routine vision, dental, and hearing healthcare services, and (3) fam ily healthcare decision-making, including familial spillover effects and intergenerational policy impacts. Her research seeks to identify policies that are effective in reduc ing healthcare disparities by race and ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and immigration status using causal inference methods . Dr. Lipton’s research has appeared in leading economics, policy, and medical journals, including the J ournal of Health Economics , Journal of Human Resources , Health Affairs , American Journal of Public Health , and JAMA Health Forum . She has been supported as a Principal Investigator by the National Institutes of Health and the William T. Grant Foundation.

sections.heading: Research and Scholarship Interests
sections.text: Lipton uses causal inference methods to examine the impacts of healthcare policies on health and economic outcomes. Current research focuses on state-level Medicaid program design, access to preventive healthcare services, and dual eligibility.

sections.heading: Biography
sections.text: Dr. Jung-Ah Lee is a nurse scientist and faculty with expertise in gerontology and healthcare systems. Her research focuses primarily on translational approach to improve care delivery and quality of life for patients and caregivers. Within this focus, a recurring theme of her work is to explore racial and ethnic disparities in quality of care. Culturally sensitive approaches to care delivery in chronic diseases including cardiovascular diseases and Alzheimer’s Disease and related dementias are a primary consideration of her research. As the principal investigator, Dr. Lee has conducted community-based participatory research starting with a needs assessment of ethnic minority older adults and dementia family caregivers. She designed and has conducted the culture and language specific dementia care program for diverse older adults and their caregivers in strong partnership with community organizations supported by several funding mechanisms including National Institute of Health/National Institute on Aging.

sections.heading: Biography
sections.text: Dr. Bender’s research focuses on the relationships between the organization of care delivery, multi-professional practice dynamics, and patient care quality and safety outcomes. Her most recent work seeks to conceptualize and quantify the efficacy of a model that integrates a new role, the clinical nurse leader (CNL), into nursing care delivery. This program of research intersects with implementation science as it explores how care interventions, context (people, things, and processes that characterize where the intervention is introduced), and implementation (processes of intervention integration) interact with each other to influence outcomes. Philosophically, Dr. Bender has focused on engaging and re-interpreting fundamental disciplinary concepts such as the nursing metaparadigm and art-science dualism using a process philosophy lens. She is also founding Director of the Center for Nursing Philosophy, which provides a platform for engaging the local, national, and international nursing community and aims to advance novel scholarship elucidating the assumptions, principles, and concepts driving the discipline.

sections.heading: Biography
sections.text: Bueno’s research focuses on the experiences of the understudied population of male caregivers for persons with Alzheimer’s Disease and related dementia, and how masculinity and gendered expectations influence their caregiver role. His previous clinical experiences as a bedside nurse have also influenced his program of research into older adult caregivers. As a nurse with clinical experience in med-surg, telemetry, and acute dialysis, Bueno had the opportunity to interact with many people with chronic illnesses. Within these experiences, he interacted with many family caregivers highlighting their important role in the long-term management of the patient’s chronic illness management. Moreover, Bueno’s experience within academia as a nursing professor has highlighted the focus on chronic illness and gerontology education as the population of older adults continue to rise and the increased need for long-term health management provided by family caregivers. The specific chronic disease of interest of Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias was influenced by having been a family caregiver himself for loved ones with the disease. To help apply his current and future research findings to improving the health of the community, he is a current volunteer community educator for the Orange County regional chapter of the Alzheimer’s Association.

sections.heading: Biography
sections.text: Dr. Sarah L. Campbell, DNP, APRN, FNP-C, is an accomplished nursing educator, scholar, and clinician who currently serves as Director of the DNP Program, Family Nurse Practitioner Concentration, and HS Associate Clinical Professor at the University of California, Irvine Sue & Bill Gross School of Nursing. She earned her Doctor of Nursing Practice from The Ohio State University, her Master of Science in Nursing from UC Irvine, and her Bachelor of Science in Nursing from California State University, Fullerton, bringing a strong academic foundation to her roles in program leadership, curriculum development, and accreditation compliance. With over two decades of clinical experience spanning telemetry nursing, heart failure coordination, house supervision, and advanced practice in internal medicine and university student health, Dr. Campbell maintains active faculty practice as a board-certified Family Nurse Practitioner, delivering patient-centered care with particular expertise in chronic disease management, geriatrics, and health promotion across the lifespan. Her scholarly contributions include peer-reviewed publications in The Nurse Practitioner, the Journal of Doctoral Nursing Practice, and Critical Care Nurse, as well as numerous podium and poster presentations at national and international conferences including NONPF, WIN, GSA, AAICNA, and APHA; she also co-authored an educational media video on Chlamydia in collaboration with Osmosis that has garnered over 61,000 views. As a funded investigator, Dr. Campbell has served as Co-Investigator on a $3.75M HRSA/GWEP TAG-TEAM grant focused on geriatric workforce enhancement and a $375,000 COVID-19 resilience grant, and was awarded a $182,000 Song Brown Grant to train DNP-FNP students for practice in underserved communities. She has chaired the DNP Programs Committee, co-chaired the Student Success Advisory Task Force, served as a UCI OEOD Sexual Harassment Advisor, and mentored over a dozen doctoral students as DNP project chair, reflecting a deep commitment to student success, interprofessional collaboration, and advancing health equity for diverse populations.

sections.heading: Biography
sections.text: Dr. Yuqing Guo’s research focuses on identifying early risk and protective factors for women’s health and developing impactful prevention and health promotion interventions by adopting a life-course perspective, collaborating with community organizations, employing a mind-body approach, and leveraging digital technologies. She has integrated these approaches to create culturally sensitive, acceptable, and scalable interventions that serve vulnerable women and their families in underserved communities. From 2018 to 2022, with National Science Foundation funding, she collaborated with computer scientists, leveraging wearable devices and mobile health applications to prospectively collect longitudinal data examining the relationships among sleep, emotional well-being, and cardiovascular health in perinatal women in home settings. In 2023, she received a pilot award from the Center for Advancing Solutions in Cardiometabolic Health, a National Institutes of Health (NIH)-funded center, to co-develop the “Healthy Sleep, Happy Hearts for Two” intervention with community organizations to reduce cardiovascular health disparities for Black and Hispanic pregnant mothers. In 2024, Dr. Guo was awarded an NIH grant to partner with data scientists in co-creating AI models and novel data integration methodologies that identify early predictors of women’s cardiometabolic health, advancing precision health through personalized prevention and intervention strategies.

sections.heading: Biography
sections.text: Dr. Jocelyn Ludlow’s expertise has influenced simulation at the national level as a member of the prebriefing and simulation design INACSL Healthcare Standards of Best Practice subcommittees. She has presented at the local and national level at simulation, nursing science, and nursing education conferences on a variety of topics including prebriefing in simulation, in situ simulation programs, and innovations in nurse education. She has been a registered nurse since 2000 and has practiced in a variety of settings with a focus on cardiac and telemetry nursing. She has been a Certified Healthcare Simulation Educator (CHSE) and a Certified Nurse Educator (CNE) since 2016, and a certified medical-surgical nurse (CMSRN) since 2017. She is also been trained in FEMA Incident Command System, AVADE and CPI De-Escalation, and Quality Matters.

sections.heading: Biography
sections.text: Dr. Tiffany Nielsen has been a registered nurse since 2008 and a nurse practitioner since 2013, serving patients in both the emergency department (ED) and primary care settings. Nielsen attended UC Irvine and graduated from the master’s Family Nurse Practitioner (FNP) Program. Upon graduation, she participated in a six-month emergency medicine training and mentorship program, where she developed the necessary skills to care for acutely ill ED patients. She later went on to obtain her Emergency Nurse Practitioner (ENP) national board certification. As part of her doctoral studies at Brandman University in 2017, she utilized a real-time model to measure ED overcrowding and developed an ambulance diversion protocol. Nielsen joined UC Irvine in 2016 and is now the Senior DNP Programs Director. She led the most recent DNP curriculum revision, launching Fall 2026. She also served as the nursing simulation coordinator from 2018-2019, advancing best practices in simulation education. She continues to engage in simulation education with the US military, including interdisciplinary mass casualty and pre-deployment simulation training. She is part of the Faculty Practice in the School and practices clinically at UC Irvine’s Student Health Center.

sections.heading: Biography
sections.text: Her findings in the US have influenced drug treatment programs, and clinic protocols and hiring practices. Her research has led enhanced uptake of vaccines, significant reduction of drug use and abuse, reductions in re-incarceration at one-year follow-up. and an increase in protective behaviors in the targeted population. In India, her successful outcomes were presented to the Indian Government and research institutes, leading to discussions about the need to financially support the nutrition of people living with HIV. Today, financial support is being provided to people living with HIV/AIDS in many states in India.  Furthermore, her research shedding light on the need for cervical cancer screening among women living with AIDS in India, has led to her new R01 from the National Cancer Institute.  Over the last 36 years, Dr Nyamathi has received continuous funding from NIH as Principal Investigator across six NIH institutes, bringing in over 40 million. She has authored over 265 peer reviewed publications.

sections.heading: Beatriz da Costa > Associate Professor
sections.text: IN MEMORIAM: BEATRIZ NORONHA DA COSTA, 1972-2012 Da Costa is an interdisciplinary artist and researcher who works at the intersection of contemporary art, science, engineering and politics. Her work takes the form of public participatory interventions, locative media, conceptual tool building, and critical writing. Da Costa has also made frequent use of wetware in her projects and has recently become interested in the potential of interspecies co-production in promoting the responsible use of natural resources and environmental sustainability. Other issues addressed in her work include the use of emergent technologies to investigate context specific configurations of social injustice, the politics of transgenic organisms, and the social repercussions of ubiquitous surveillance technologies.  Through her work da Costa examines the role of the artist as a political actor engaged in technoscientific discourses. This topic is addressed in an anthology she co-edited with her colleague Kavita Philip entitled Tactical Biopolitics: Theory & Practice life.science.art, (MIT Press, 2008). Da Costa is a co-founder of Preemptive Media, an arts, activism and technology group, and a former collaborator of Critical Art Ensemble (2000-2005). She has exhibited and lectured both nationally and internationally at venues such as the Andy Warhol Museum, Exit Art Gallery, the Zentrum fuer Kunst und Medien in Germany, SONAR in Barcelona, the Saidye Bronfman Centre for the Arts in Montreal, and the Natural History Museum in London. She is a Creative Capital grantee of 2009. Recent media coverage of her work has appeared in the New York Times, the Los Angeles Times, Reuters, CBS Evening News, BBC, CBC and the New Scientist. Da Costa has received grants from the Durfee Foundation, the Inter-Society for Electronic Arts, and the University of California Institute for the Research in the Arts. She has also received an Honorary Mention from the Adobe Emergent Artists Award and been nominated twice for the Rockefeller New Media Arts grant. Preemptive Media received the Social Sculpture Commission from Eyebeam and the Lower Manhattan Cultural Council, as well as funding from Franklin Furnace, Turbulence, the Experimental Television Center, and the Beall Center for Art and Technology. Da Costa spent two years as an exchange student at Carnegie Mellon University while completing her MFA thesis.

sections.text: Conventional small molecule discovery is driven by high-throughput screening (HTS) centers. These centers are stuffed with expensive robotics designed to move microplates between various operations, such as compound dispensing, assay dispensing, incubation and optical screening. With well over 50,000 selective small molecule modulators required to probe human biology alone, our rate of discovery/cost (200 probes, 3 years, $400 million) must improve to reach this important goal. We have engineered an ultra-miniaturized and integrated microfluidic platform that dispenses with the robotics, microplates, and conventional compound libraries, and all of the costs associated therein. We envision an HTS instrument that can operate in any laboratory using DNA-encoded libraries, and consume minute quantities of precious screening reagents and cell lines. HTS campaigns of tomorrow using this platform will be as distributed and inexpensive as DNA sequencing is today, in pursuit of the original predicted outcome of the Human Genome Project: the ability to translate genomic sequence into therapeutics.

sections.heading: Biography
sections.text: Dr. Cassidie Thomas brings over a decade of clinical and leadership expertise across diverse practice settings, including school health, reproductive endocrinology and infertility, labor and delivery, and pediatric intensive care. Her work in school health encompasses initiatives in policy development, health education, research, and quality improvement, contributing to meaningful advancements in school communities. Dr. Thomas serves as a leader in the Private, Independent, and Parochial School branch of the National Association of School Nurses, where she is committed to fostering mentorship and collaboration among school nursing professionals. Her scholarship focuses on empowering school nurses through evidence-based practices and advancing school nursing to support the long-term emotional and physical well-being of students. She earned her Doctor of Nursing Practice (DNP) degree with a Family Nurse Practitioner focus from the UC Irvine Sue & Bill Gross School of Nursing. A passionate educator, Dr. Thomas is dedicated to inspiring and mentoring the next generation of nurses. In 2024, she joined the faculty of the UC Irvine Sue & Bill Gross School of Nursing, where she currently teaches in the Prelicensure Program.

sections.heading: Current Projects/Studies
sections.text: Advancing Fungal Disease Epidemiology through Multilevel Modeling and Data Integration Funder: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIH K01 Career Development Award) Collaborators: Justin Remais (UC Berkeley), Jon Zelner (University of Michigan), Children’s Mercy Hospital (Kansas City), Becky Staiger (UC Berkeley), Sara Tartof (Kaiser Permanente) This project investigates how social, structural, environmental, and healthcare factors contribute to disparities in invasive fungal diseases across the US. By integrating national electronic health record data with environmental and community-level datasets, the project seeks to identify the contextual drivers of fungal disease risk and outcomes and improve our understanding of the processes that generate infectious disease inequities. Disaster Resilience and Population Health Collaborators: University of California Disaster Resilience Network Executive Committee and partner organizations across the University of California This work brings together researchers and community partners across the UC system to develop collaborative research and education initiatives that advance disaster resilience and population health.
